label: Person
name: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky
summary:
Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky (1840–1893) was a Russian composer of the Romantic era whose works—including the ballets 'Swan Lake' (1877), 'The Sleeping Beauty' (1890), and 'The Nutcracker' (1892)—are among the most frequently performed compositions in the classical repertoire worldwide.

Trained at the St. Petersburg Conservatory, Tchaikovsky fused Western European musical forms with Russian melodic sensibility. His six symphonies, three piano concertos, and the Violin Concerto in D major combine structural sophistication with an emotional directness that appeals to audiences universally. The 1812 Overture, with its cannon fire, remains one of the most recognisable pieces of classical music.

Tchaikovsky's personal life was marked by inner turmoil. His brief, disastrous marriage in 1877 and the patronage of Nadezhda von Meck—a wealthy widow who supported him financially for 13 years on condition they never meet—reflected his struggle with his homosexuality in a deeply conservative society.

He died in St. Petersburg at age 53, days after the premiere of his Sixth Symphony ('Pathétique')—a work of devastating emotional power that he considered his finest. Whether he died of cholera or suicide remains debated. Stravinsky called him 'the most Russian of us all.'
